newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU budget pact seen test of Franco-German alliance.
newsitem.headline: EMU budget pact seen test of Franco-German alliance.

text.p: A European pact designed to ensure discipline inside the future single currency is shaping up to be the first test of how the new French government and Germany will co-operate on the economic and monetary union (EMU).

The new French Socialist government wasted no time since winning the general elections on Sunday in declaring its unhappiness with the accord, seen by the European Union as essential to the credibility of the future common currency.

French Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande told Reuters Financial Television that the government did not want sanctions included in the "stability and growth pact", hammered out by European leaders last December and due for final approval later this month at a summit in Amsterdam.
"We want to be sure that sanctions will not be applied if the main objectives are not reached," Hollande said without elaborating further.
The statements led some analysts to believe France might seek a revision of the accord, but others said it was only posturing while realising the costs of going back to the subject would be enormous.
Under the pact, governments inside EMU would be penalised if they allowed their annual budget deficits to rise above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

Although the agreement is considered by many to be a watered-down version of a stricter blueprint proposed by Germany, it is an element of the EMU process which many believe enhances the project's ultimate success.
To reopen negotiations now could create a sharp rift between Bonn and Paris, the consequences of which analysts say is nearly impossible to gauge.
"This is significant in the sense that it is the first substantial difference between Germany and France over EMU," said Martin Brookes, economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
"It could potentially unsettle public opinion in Germany if there is a sense that the politicians in France are attempting to wrestle control over EMU away from the bankers."
In its election manifesto, the Socialist party laid down various conditions for the common currency, the euro, including a European economic government to counterbalance an independent central bank.
